analysis.one_liner: Outlaws the pesticide chlorpyrifos, canceling its registration and banning its residue on food.
analysis.headline: The chlorpyrifos ban drew 118 cosponsors, including one Republican, but never got a hearing or a vote in two House committees before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Chlorpyrifos is a widely used farm insecticide that the EPA's own scientists concluded can harm children's brain development at exposures people actually experience, including from residues on food and drift into homes near sprayed fields. The bill would have done immediately what the agency had spent years litigating over: cancel every registered use, revoke the legal allowances for chlorpyrifos residue on food, ban the sale and use of existing stock, and bar the EPA from ever re-registering it.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, pregnant women, farmworkers, and people living near treated fields. Exposure to chlorpyrifos is linked to reduced IQ, attention problems, and developmental delays in children, and farmworkers and rural residents face the highest exposures. The bill would have removed it from food and fields outright, with no phase-in period.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children, farmworkers, and families near sprayed fields

how_it_helps.text: Declares chlorpyrifos to cause unreasonable adverse effects and directs the EPA to cancel the registration of all of its uses on the day the bill becomes law.
Requires the EPA to revoke the legal tolerances that allow chlorpyrifos residue on food, making any chlorpyrifos on food illegal.
Prohibits the continued sale and use of existing stocks of chlorpyrifos, rather than allowing inventory to be sold off after the ban.
Bars the EPA from reregistering chlorpyrifos, preventing the product from being reintroduced later.

analysis.who_pays: The manufacturer loses the entire U.S. registration for a flagship product, including the right to sell inventory already on shelves. Growers of crops that leaned on chlorpyrifos for insect control, such as some fruit, tree nut, and alfalfa operations, lose a cheap and effective tool and would need substitutes or extra treatments, some of which could be passed on in food prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill is deliberately blunt: cancellation is effective on the day of enactment with no phase-out period, which gives growers no transition runway and the ban on existing stocks forces disposal of inventory on hand.

Growers of a few crops argued chlorpyrifos was the last effective or economical control for certain pests, so the ban imposes real pest-management costs on those operations even as it removes a neurotoxin from food and fields.
A unilateral statutory ban forecloses the ordinary EPA risk-benefit process, which is a cost in good governance terms even for supporters who agree with the outcome.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case was strong: the EPA's own risk assessments under both prior and current administrations had found unsafe exposures for children and workers, and the eventual outcome proved the point — the EPA banned chlorpyrifos on food in 2021 under a court order. The costs fall on one manufacturer and on a subset of growers, and are real but narrow; the main honest criticism of the bill is its lack of a phase-in, not its goal.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Agriculture and Energy and Commerce Committees on the day it was introduced, sent to subcommittees a month later, and then sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velázquez introduced the Ban Toxic Pesticides Act of 2019 on January 3, 2019, the first day of the 116th Congress.
The bill was referred to the Agriculture Committee and, additionally, to the Energy and Commerce Committee.
By late February 2019 it had been sent to the Biotechnology, Horticulture, and Research Subcommittee and the Environment and Climate Change Subcommittee.

It gathered 118 cosponsors — 117 of 231 House Democrats and 1 of 197 House Republicans — but neither committee took it up, and no vote ever occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chlorpyrifos maker Corteva and the growers still using the product kept a legal market for it through the end of the Congress, and no vote was ever recorded on the ban. Children and farmworkers continued to bear the exposure the bill would have ended; the protection only arrived later, from the EPA and the courts rather than from Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The pesticide maker and growers still using it

for.name: Rep. Nydia Velázquez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cancel all chlorpyrifos registrations and ban its residue on food.

for.name: 1 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republican support.

against.name: Rep. Collin Peterson
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral on day one and took no further action on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the secondary referral and took no further action on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.name: Trump administration EPA
against.what_they_did: In 2017 the EPA declined to carry out its own earlier proposed ban on chlorpyrifos food uses, keeping the pesticide legal and removing the immediate regulatory pressure that might have moved Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 117 of 231 House Democrats signed on, versus 1 of 197 Republicans — and the bill died in committee without a roll call that could have shown more.

industries.industry: Pesticide manufacturers (Corteva, maker of Lorsban-brand chlorpyrifos)
industries.note: The bill cancels the entire U.S. registration and bans even existing stock, wiping out the domestic market for its flagship insecticide. Keeping the product legal meant the continued neurotoxin exposure the EPA's own science had flagged, so its interest ran against the families and workers the bill protected.

Farmers lose a low-cost insect-control tool on some crops with limited substitutes in the short run, a genuine cost. Their interest in keeping the chemical legal nonetheless sat on the opposite side of the children's-health protections the bill provided.
Removing chlorpyrifos creates demand for substitute pest-control products, and their gain comes with the removal of a hazard rather than at the public's expense.
